title: Signal · Thursday 12 November
overview: McKinsey finds Swiss banks highly profitable but short of AI scale, Nvidia's board weighs Jensen Huang's future, and the SNB sees no credit crunch.

top.headline: McKinsey finds Swiss banks more profitable than peers but short of AI scale
top.summary: Banks worldwide raised profits by 7 percent to a record USD 1.3 trillion last year, McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review 2026 found, and Swiss banks did even better on the back of wealth management. Of about 46,000 customers surveyed in 13 countries, excluding Switzerland, 23 percent use generative AI for money matters, and 74 percent of those use ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
top.background: McKinsey calls the Swiss financial centre highly fragmented, with many smaller banks unable to match the AI budgets of the largest international groups.
top.why: Mid-sized Swiss banks risk losing the first conversation about money to general assistants, although 62 percent of AI users would still rather be advised by their own bank.
top.watch_next: The Swiss Finance Institute's annual meeting in Zurich on 12 November is devoted to the impact of AI on finance.

top.headline: Update: Nvidia's board meets on Jensen Huang's future after a second affair report
top.summary: Nvidia's board is preparing to remove chief executive Jensen Huang and could meet as soon as 11 November to decide, according to the Wall Street Journal, as reported by TechCrunch. The New York Times reported on 11 November that Huang had also had an affair with an executive who reports to him, and Nvidia shares fell about 8 percent in after-hours trading.
top.background: Huang admitted on 8 November to an affair with a woman US intelligence believes is a Chinese spy. He has led Nvidia for 33 years and has no obvious successor.
top.why: Nvidia makes the chips behind most of the AI build-out, so its leadership matters to AI infrastructure plans, chip export politics and a large weight in client equity portfolios.
top.watch_next: Nvidia reports third-quarter results on 17 November.

top.headline: SNB sees no credit crunch and confirms its growth forecasts
top.summary: At its annual discussion with the Federal Council on 11 November, the Swiss National Bank said domestic lending has kept growing over the past ten years, including after the collapse of Credit Suisse, and that it sees no signs of a credit crunch. It still expects growth of 1.5 to 2 percent this year and around 1.5 percent in 2027, according to finews.
top.why: For Swiss banks, the assessment points to steady lending conditions into 2027, with energy prices, trade policy and exchange rates named as the main risks.
top.background: Inflation has risen from 0.6 percent in May to 1.5 percent in October, mainly on oil prices, but remains inside the SNB's 0 to 2 percent range.
top.watch_next: The SNB's next monetary policy assessment is on 10 December.

items.headline: Aladdin study finds AI widespread in investment firms but rarely used in decisions
items.summary: A Forrester Consulting study for BlackRock's Aladdin, polling more than 300 senior decision-makers at asset managers, insurers, pension funds, banks and wealth managers, found 87 percent have deployed AI or set up use cases. Most use it only for operational efficiency; the main obstacles are employee readiness (61 percent), AI talent (58 percent) and data infrastructure (55 percent).
items.why: Wealth managers aiming to put AI into portfolio decisions will be paced by data foundations that most firms describe as incomplete.

items.headline: Selma hires former Swiss Life chief Bruno Pfister to expand AI retirement advice
items.summary: Digital wealth manager Selma has appointed Bruno Pfister, Swiss Life's group chief executive from 2008 to 2014, as strategic adviser for its AI-driven pension advice, finews reported. Selma says more than 100,000 people retire in Switzerland each year and about CHF 17 billion is paid out to them as lump sums annually.
items.why: Retirement lump sums are a large, advice-heavy pool where banks' advisers now meet AI-led competitors with senior insurance credibility.

items.headline: Swiss Life grows premiums 8 percent as third-party asset inflows slow
items.summary: Swiss Life said fee income rose 8 percent in local currencies to CHF 2.04 billion in the first nine months and premiums 8 percent to CHF 17.4 billion, with Swiss premiums up 15 percent to CHF 9.4 billion. Net new money in third-party asset management fell to CHF 8.5 billion from CHF 15 billion, according to finews.
items.why: Occupational pension money is driving Swiss insurers' growth while their asset managers find third-party money harder to win.

items.headline: Allianz reports a record EUR 14.1 billion nine-month operating profit and raises guidance
items.summary: Allianz said operating profit for the first nine months reached a record EUR 14.1 billion, up from EUR 13.1 billion a year earlier. It raised the upper end of its 2026 target, set at EUR 17.4 billion plus or minus EUR 1 billion, to around EUR 18.6 billion, barring major natural catastrophes or capital market events.
items.why: Europe's largest insurer sets the bar for Zurich Insurance, which publishes its third-quarter update on 12 November.

items.headline: Ten-year Treasury yields top 5 percent as Fed's Waller floats a larger hike
items.summary: US consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in October from September, above the 0.3 percent expected. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on 10 November that a 50-basis-point rise was possible, though futures still price a 25-point move on 9 December as most likely, according to finews.
items.why: Higher US rates support banks' interest income but weigh on the technology valuations that dominate many client portfolios.

items.headline: China's wealthy declare USD 24 billion in back taxes on offshore trusts
items.summary: Wealthy Chinese have declared more than RMB 160 billion (USD 24 billion) in back taxes tied to offshore trusts, and the authorities collected more than RMB 120 billion of it in October, WealthBriefing reported, citing Xinhua and Bloomberg. China said in July it would formally tax offshore trusts set up by its citizens.
items.why: The campaign tests the offshore trust structures that wealth centres from Hong Kong to Switzerland have long serviced for Chinese families.

items.headline: OpenAI's quarterly revenue passed USD 10 billion for the first time, Bloomberg reports
items.summary: OpenAI's third-quarter revenue crossed USD 10 billion, Bloomberg reported citing anonymous sources, according to TechCrunch. That would be an almost 50 percent jump from the USD 6.7 billion reported for the second quarter, with the adjusted operating margin narrowing from minus 150 percent to minus 109 percent.
items.why: The figure narrows the gap with Anthropic, which TechCrunch notes reported USD 17 billion in third-quarter revenue, as both labs compete for enterprise budgets.

items.headline: Databricks turns Genie into an autonomous coworker and plugs it into Claude and ChatGPT
items.summary: Databricks said Genie now runs long tasks on its own within guardrails, drawing on Genie Ontology for certified business definitions, while Unity Gateway lets administrators control tool access, trace actions and cap spending. Genie plugins now work natively in ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Grok Bot, with other agents reaching it through an MCP server.
items.why: Banks with data in Databricks get a governed route for staff assistants to query it, with definitions and permissions enforced at the source.
items.for_your_skills: For your skills: with the Genie plugin in Claude, Discovery could pull a client's certified figures from Databricks when sizing benefits, where the client grants access.

items.headline: Google launches a Gemini Decisions API for fast, scored yes-or-no and rubric judgements
items.summary: Google introduced the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1, which evaluates up to 1,000 yes-or-no, multiple-choice and rubric questions in a single pass across text, images, audio, video and PDFs. It returns confidence scores and is aimed at routing queries, grading content and checking policy rules.
items.why: Compliance and operations teams get a cheaper building block for checks that today send every document through a full model.

items.headline: Microsoft fixes about 1,090 vulnerabilities, including an Outlook flaw already being exploited
items.summary: Microsoft's November security updates cover about 1,090 vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, Exchange Server, Azure and .NET, according to Inside IT, citing the Zero Day Initiative. An Outlook flaw that leaks users' NTLM hashes is under active attack, and a critical Windows Search bug can be triggered when Exchange indexes a crafted attachment.
items.why: Bank IT teams running Exchange and Outlook face an unusually heavy patch cycle, with 30 flaws the Zero Day Initiative calls potentially wormable.

items.headline: CoreWeave asks customers to prepay as it funds AI capacity without unsecured debt
items.summary: CoreWeave reported third-quarter revenue of USD 3.66 billion, up 168 percent, with a USD 709 million net loss and USD 846 million in interest expense, according to TechCrunch. It is asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts and pursuing shorter deals, and said it would not use the unsecured debt market at current yields.
items.why: Banks lending to AI infrastructure see credit quality tied more closely to the customer contracts behind each facility.

say_it_today: Three in four bank customers who use AI for money questions do it on ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, yet 62 percent would rather be advised by their own bank, McKinsey found. The trust is still with the banks; the first conversation is moving elsewhere.
